lesson.title: Same Pot, Same Phase: Homogeneous Catalysis
lesson.summary: In homogeneous catalysis, the catalyst occupies the same physical phase as the reactants, most often all dissolved together in one solution, so it can interact directly with reactant molecules throughout the mixture.
lesson.body:
A homogeneous catalyst is defined by phase: it is in the same phase as the reactants it is speeding up, whether that means everything is dissolved in one liquid solution or everything is mixed together as gases. Because catalyst and reactants are uniformly distributed through the same volume, they can collide with each other anywhere in the mixture, and catalysis happens through direct, molecule to molecule interactions rather than at some kind of boundary or surface.

The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, the same reaction discussed with the solid catalyst manganese dioxide in the catalysis chapter, can also be catalyzed homogeneously by iodide ion, I minus, dissolved right in the same aqueous solution as the peroxide. The mechanism runs through two steps. First, H2O2 plus I minus forms H2O plus IO minus, hypoiodite ion. Second, H2O2 plus IO minus forms H2O plus O2 plus I minus. Adding these together, the IO minus cancels since it is produced in the first step and consumed in the second, making it the intermediate, and the I minus cancels out to a net catalytic role, appearing as a reactant in step one and being regenerated as a product in step two. The overall result is exactly the same as before, 2H2O2 forming 2H2O plus O2, but now every species involved, the peroxide, the iodide catalyst, and the water produced, sits in the same aqueous phase, which is what makes this a homogeneous catalyst rather than a heterogeneous one like the solid MnO2 version.

This connects to what you know about solutions: homogeneous catalysis very often takes place in liquid solution, aqueous or otherwise, though it can also happen in a well mixed gas phase, such as certain gas phase reactions in the atmosphere where a dissolved or gaseous species catalyzes a reaction among other gases. One real advantage of homogeneous catalysis is that, since the catalyst is uniformly mixed with the reactants at the molecular level, every catalyst molecule has equal access to reactant molecules, which tends to give clean, well behaved kinetics that are relatively easy to study and model. A real practical drawback shows up afterward: because the catalyst ends up mixed into the same phase as the product, separating it back out, say recovering the iodide catalyst from the water and oxygen produced, can be more difficult and costly than it would be if the catalyst had simply been a solid sitting apart from a liquid or gas mixture, which is exactly the kind of separation advantage heterogeneous catalysis offers.

The same pattern shows up throughout organic and industrial chemistry. Acid catalyzed ester hydrolysis in aqueous solution, where H plus ions speed up the breakdown of an ester into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, is homogeneous for the same reason: the acid catalyst and the ester reactant are both dissolved in the same aqueous phase.
